articles.title: Cronkeyshaw Common bonfire night proves a huge success as quiet fireworks light up the sky
articles.excerpt: Quiet fireworks set to music including Queen’s Don’t Stop Me Now have delighted the crowd at Cronkeyshaw Common, with little to no traffic disruption reported so far.
articles.content_html:
Cronkeyshaw Common’s bonfire night has so far proved a huge success, with a colourful fireworks display set to music and little to no traffic disruption reported around the event.

An eyewitness report to Rochdale Daily described an evening enjoyed by those watching, with “quiet” fireworks lighting up the sky to a soundtrack including Queen’s Don’t Stop Me Now.

The reduced-noise display was intended to help limit distress to wildlife and people who find loud fireworks difficult, while keeping the spectacle and shared enjoyment of bonfire night.

The photograph accompanying this update captures the crowd watching bright trails and bursts of colour above the common in Syke.

Despite temporary road closures and parking restrictions around the site, the report from the evening so far is of little to no traffic disruption. That is an observation from the event, rather than a borough-wide traffic assessment.

The free event on Wednesday 4 November was organised by Rochdale Borough Council, following this week’s displays in Middleton and Heywood. The advertised programme ran from 6pm to 10pm, with the bonfire scheduled for 7pm and the reduced-noise fireworks set to music for 7.30pm.

Road closures and parking restrictions were scheduled from 4pm to 9pm around Greenbank Road, Dewhirst Road, Fieldhouse Road, Joy Street and Binns Nook Road, with additional waiting restrictions on nearby streets.

There is no parking on the common. Visitors are asked to remain considerate of residents and keep access clear as they leave.

articles.title: Littleborough Christmas lights: Church Street restrictions confirmed for 28 November
articles.excerpt: Church Street restrictions are planned for Littleborough's Christmas lights event on Saturday 28 November, including a daytime waiting ban and an afternoon road closure.
articles.content_html:
Drivers and visitors heading into Littleborough for the Christmas lights event on Saturday, 28 November 2026 should plan around temporary restrictions on Church Street.

Rochdale Borough Council's published traffic notice says a road closure will operate from 1.30pm until 7pm. A prohibition on waiting is due to run from noon until 7pm on the same day, meaning parking arrangements will change before the road closure starts.

The notice identifies Church Street and Peel Street as the location of the restriction. Its wording for the precise starting junction is unclear, because it describes Church Street as beginning at a junction with Church Street itself. Residents who need access to a particular property should check the official notice and seek clarification from the council rather than relying on an assumed boundary.

The council lists Church Street, Morgan Street, Peel Street and Station Road as the alternative route. Drivers should follow temporary signs on the day, as the published notice does not provide a street-by-street map of how each turning will operate.

The restrictions are for the Littleborough Christmas Lights Event 2026, which the council has confirmed for Saturday, 28 November. The traffic notice does not give the entertainment timetable or the exact time of the lights switch-on, so those details should not be assumed from the road closure hours.

Anyone planning to visit shops, businesses or homes around the affected streets should allow extra time, particularly during the afternoon and early evening. Those with deliveries or access requirements may wish to confirm arrangements ahead of the event.

The full council notice, including the restriction wording and alternative route, can be checked at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2626/littleborough-christmas-lights-event-2026-road-closures-in-littleborough-on-28-november-2026.

articles.title: New Ukrainian GCSE welcomed for Rochdale pupils
articles.excerpt: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has welcomed plans for a Ukrainian GCSE, with teaching expected from September 2028 and first exams in 2029.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale pupils are set to have the opportunity to study for a new Ukrainian GCSE, with teaching expected to begin in September 2028 and the first exams planned for summer 2029.

Rochdale MP Paul Waugh welcomed the announcement, saying it would give children who fled Russia’s war the chance to gain a qualification in Ukrainian.

In a statement shared alongside a photograph of a group holding a Ukrainian flag, Mr Waugh said Ukrainian child refugees in the UK had been told to study Russian at GCSE as an alternative to Ukrainian. He described that situation as unacceptable for children who had fled the war.

“I'm so proud to have such a brilliant Ukrainian community in Rochdale, and I'm glad to have helped make this possible for them,” he said.

The qualification will be developed by AQA and will be open to all pupils, giving young Ukrainians a way to gain recognition for their language skills and maintain a connection to their heritage.

It is expected to be available in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Like other modern foreign language GCSEs, it will assess listening, speaking, reading and writing, alongside the cultural and historical context of the language.

The timetable remains subject to Ofqual approval. The national announcement does not yet set out which individual Rochdale schools will offer the course.

For families in Rochdale’s Ukrainian community, the planned qualification offers a future route to formal recognition of a language that is an important part of their identity.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards contract for Empty Homes Leasing Programme
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for the GM Empty Homes TA Leasing Programme, aimed at providing temporary accommodation for families.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for the GM Empty Homes Temporary Accommodation (TA) Leasing Programme. This framework contract is set for an initial term of four years or until the contract value reaches £3.5 million, whichever comes first.

The programme aims to lease or acquire 2-4 bedroom homes to provide temporary accommodation for families that the Council has a duty to support under sections 188, 190, or 193 of the Housing Act.

The initiative seeks to incentivise property owners with homes that have been empty for six months or more to bring them back into use, thereby reducing the costs associated with temporary accommodation.

In addition to the framework contract, a call-off contract has also been awarded to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for a minimum of 20 to a maximum of 32 properties. The value of this call-off contract is not guaranteed, reflecting the flexible nature of the agreement.

This initiative is significant for Rochdale as it addresses the pressing need for safe and secure accommodation for families facing housing challenges. By utilising empty homes, the Council aims to improve housing availability while managing costs effectively.

The libraries also offer books and other reading activities, and the council maintains a wider events directory for families who cannot attend either session. A free library session does not require families to buy materials or tickets for the activities described above.

articles.title: Rochdale Council leaves door open for Hopwood Hall reconciliation after court ruling
articles.excerpt: Following a recent High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has expressed willingness to engage with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, which has been a point of contention since the termination of their agreement in 2024.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has indicated a willingness to engage in discussions with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate their agreement.

This development comes after a two-day trial at Manchester Civil Justice Centre in September, where the court ruled that the council acted lawfully in ending the exclusivity agreement with DePree, who had sought to purchase the historic site for £1.

The council's option agreement with DePree, which began in 2017, was terminated in October 2024, leading to a legal dispute. DePree, who claims ancestral ties to the hall, believed he had a binding agreement to purchase the property.

However, the court found that a planning approval granted in 2022 did not trigger the option to buy the hall for the nominal fee.

In response to the court's decision, DePree has issued an open letter to the council, outlining his terms for a potential resolution.

He expressed a desire for constructive dialogue and transparency regarding the council's decisions, including a request for the release of documents related to the handling of the hall's management. DePree has suggested that an independent review could help clarify the situation and facilitate discussions.

Council leader Neil Emmott reiterated that the council's 'door is always open' for DePree to present a viable plan for Hopwood Hall's future.

Both parties have acknowledged that the costly court battle could have been avoided, and there is hope for an amicable resolution that benefits the community and preserves the historic site.
articles.social_headline: Rochdale Council is open to talks with Hopwood DePree about Hopwood Hall's future.

At the October 15, 2026 public council meeting, you stated that your ‘door is always open’ and ‘Rochdale council is willing to listen’ if I come forward with a sustainable plan, following the council’s unexpected termination of our community-led rescue in 2024. ‌ View 4 Images An aerial view shows Hopwood Hall, the ancestral home of US film producer Hopwood DePree, that dates from the 15th century, which he is in the process of restoring, in Middleton, northern England on November 28, 2022. - As a child, Hopwood DePree had heard family stories about owning a castle in England but never took them too seriously. That was until he tracked down the 15th century castle with 16 rooms in the countryside near Manchester. In 2017 the American quit California to work full-time on restoring the building -- a task that keeps him very busy. - TO GO WITH AFP STORY BY Caroline TAIX (Photo by OLI SCARFF / AFP) / TO GO WITH AFP STORY BY Caroline TAIX (Photo by OLI SCARFF/AFP via Getty Images) “I would welcome constructive discussions but they must begin with a clear explanation of why our previous proposal was rejected. Nearly two years after our heritage team was locked out, the council still has not provided meaningful answers and continues to refuse to release documents and communications about decisions taken. ‌ “Despite our challenges, I remain open to constructive dialogue, including an independently moderated public forum where councillors, volunteers and residents can address concerns and explore Hopwood Hall’s future. “Given the time-sensitive nature of our legal options, we must reserve our rights. However, this should not prevent prompt, productive discussion aimed at reaching a resolution without further litigation. My hope is that sums that will otherwise be expended on legal costs can be better used for the benefit of the Hall. ‌ “My commitment remains to see Hopwood Hall rescued, restored and enjoyed by future generations. I hope you will respond openly to these requests.” Currently, Mr DePree’s legal team has another two weeks to decide if they want to appeal the High Court decision made in September. ‌ What the council and its leader has said A council spokesperson said: “The council successfully defended the High Court claim concerning Hopwood Hall and, as the period in which the claimant may seek permission to appeal has not yet expired, it would not be appropriate to comment further on the proceedings or the issues raised in the open letter at this stage. “We remain focused on securing a sustainable future for Hopwood Hall, once the legal process has concluded.” ‌ After being quizzed on the next steps for Hopwood Hall previously, Coun Emmott did not clarify a specific use for its future, but vowed to bring it back into use for the wider community. At the latest town hall meeting, Coun Emmott said: “The High Court’s judgment in relation to Hopwood Hall does not necessarily mark the end of the legal process. ‌ “Mr DePree has the right to seek permission to appeal the decision. The court has directed that any application for permission to appeal must be lodged by November 18, 2026, although there is scope for this deadline to be extended to November 28, 2026. View 4 Images Rochdale council leader, Neil Emmott (Image: Kenny Brown | Manchester Evening News) ‌ “The council was awarded total costs of £114,000. I can confirm these monies will be reinvested into the project. As part of any appeal process, Mr DePree would be required to make a payment into court of approximately £80,000 towards Rochdale council’s legal costs. “Should Mr DePree pursue an appeal, he would first need to obtain the court’s permission to proceed. This would require him to demonstrate that the proposed appeal has a real prospect of success or that there is another compelling reason for it to be heard. ‌ “Only Mr DePree and his legal advisers can determine whether an appeal is pursued. It is understandable that emotions remain strong within the local community, particularly among those volunteers who have dedicated considerable time and effort to the Hopwood Hall project. However, the council cannot move forward until the matter of the appeal is settled. “I can, though, assure the council and the people of Middleton that we remain focussed on the future of Hopwood Hall and the opportunities that now exist to secure its long-term restoration and preservation. More than £1.6m has already been spent on repairs to the hall by the council and Historic England. We will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. articles.title: Eighth arrest in property damage investigation covering Rochdale
articles.excerpt: GMP says Rochdale is among six areas where properties were damaged during October. A 29-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.
articles.content_html:
An investigation into damage to properties in Rochdale and five other Greater Manchester areas has led to an eighth arrest, police have said.

A 29-year-old man was arrested on Monday morning, 2 November, on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage. Greater Manchester Police said he was being questioned in connection with damage caused during October.

The force said the wider investigation concerns houses in multiple occupation, known as HMOs, and properties mistaken for HMOs.

Since 5 October, police have been made aware of damage to buildings in Rochdale, Salford, Tameside, Stockport, Bolton and Wigan. The latest release does not identify the Rochdale properties or give a separate total for the borough.

GMP said the arrest brought the number of people detained during the investigation to eight. GMP has not given the location of the latest arrest.

Enquiries are continuing. Anyone with information that could help the investigation can contact police on 101 or report it online at https://www.gmp.police.uk/.

Information can also be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

The arrest is not a finding of guilt. The man is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

articles.title: Rochdale to review future primary and secondary school place needs on 24 November
articles.excerpt: The council's forward plan schedules reports on primary places through 2030 and secondary places through 2031, alongside high-needs investment, for its 24 November cabinet meeting.
articles.content_html:
How many school places will Rochdale need in the next few years? The borough council has scheduled separate reports on primary and secondary capacity for consideration by its cabinet on Tuesday, 24 November 2026.

The council's official forward plan lists 'Need for Primary School Places 2027–2030' and 'Need for Secondary School Places 2027–2031'. Both are assigned to lead officer Fay Davies and marked as open rather than exempt items. The same meeting is due to consider a 'High Needs Capital and Investment 2026' report, which is marked part exempt because of financial or commercially sensitive information.

These are proposed decision dates, not announcements of new schools, closures, catchment changes or a confirmed number of places. The forward plan identifies subjects the council expects to consider, but it does not itself contain the detailed forecasts, recommendations or decisions. Those must be checked in the published agenda papers when available.

The timing matters to parents thinking ahead to admissions in 2027 and beyond. School-place planning looks at the capacity required across future years, while an individual child's application and allocation follow the separate admissions process. The council's published secondary-school application deadline for September 2027 entry was Saturday, 31 October 2026; families who missed it should use the council's admissions guidance rather than assuming the forthcoming cabinet report changes the deadline.

Other open items listed for 24 November include additional highway maintenance funding, a community asset transfer policy and the calculation of the 2027/28 Council Tax base. The plan also schedules a capital programme for consultation and discretionary fees and charges for consultation for 30 November, with the borough Local Plan publication plan listed for 17 December. These dates can change and do not establish that any proposal has been approved.

Rochdale Daily will check the agenda and published reports before reporting any school-place figures, recommended changes or financial commitments. Residents can read the official forward plan and subsequent meeting papers through the council's democratic services website.

Primary source: Rochdale Borough Council, Notice of Key Decisions and Private Items, 1 October 2026 to 31 January 2027: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgListPlanItems.aspx?PlanId=1453.

articles.title: Hopwood Hall College partners with Rochdale AFC to enhance football education
articles.excerpt: Hopwood Hall College has announced a partnership with Rochdale AFC to offer a new BTEC Sport with Football qualification starting in September 2027, providing students with unique opportunities in the football industry.
articles.content_html:
Hopwood Hall College has teamed up with Rochdale AFC to launch a new BTEC Sport with Football qualification, set to begin in September 2027.

This initiative aims to cultivate a new generation of talent for the football industry, providing students with practical training and educational opportunities.

Students enrolling in this programme will benefit from weekly training sessions led by professional coaches from Rochdale AFC. They will also have the chance to attend one free game each term at the Crown Oil Arena, further enhancing their connection to the sport.

The partnership is expected to bolster the college's boys' and girls' football teams, paving the way for greater success on the pitch.

Key figures involved in this initiative include Kris Robinson, Director of Curriculum at Hopwood Hall College, and George Delves, Head of Football Operations and Administration at Rochdale AFC.

This collaboration not only enriches the educational experience for students but also strengthens the ties between the college and the local football community. As the programme develops, it will provide young people passionate about football with exciting new pathways into the industry.

articles.title: Zambrero to give away free burritos at new Mellor Street restaurant in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Zambrero will hand out hundreds of free burritos and bowls from 11am to 2pm on Thursday 12 November to mark its new Mellor Street restaurant, which opened in September.
articles.content_html:
Zambrero is giving away free burritos and bowls at its new Mellor Street restaurant in Rochdale next week, as a thank-you to the town six weeks after it opened.

The Free Burrito Day takes place on Thursday 12 November, from 11am to 2pm. The company says it will hand out hundreds of freshly made burritos and bowls during the three-hour window, and is advising people to arrive early to avoid the queues. Zambrero's resident scratch DJ, NC, will be playing hip hop and crowd favourites throughout.

The restaurant opened on 25 September and is Zambrero's first site in Rochdale. It offers dine-in, takeaway and delivery, has seating for 18, and is close to the town centre and local colleges. According to the company, the opening has created six jobs.

The menu centres on burritos and bowls, alongside tacos, nachos and quesadillas, made to order at the counter. Customers can choose from slow-cooked fillings, salad, rice, beans and toppings, and there are vegetarian, vegan and halal options.

The site also brings the chain's Plate 4 Plate scheme to Rochdale, under which a meal is donated to someone in need for every burrito or bowl bought. Zambrero says the scheme has provided more than 110 million meals worldwide.

Damian Bennett, Zambrero's development agent for Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire, said: "We've had a fantastic response since opening our doors in Rochdale and this Free Burrito Day is our way of thanking the local community for its support. We can't wait to welcome residents, students and local workers to come along, enjoy a free burrito or bowl and experience what Zambrero is all about."

He added that every burrito and bowl given away on the day, and bought afterwards, would count towards the Plate 4 Plate programme.

Rochdale is Zambrero's 18th UK opening since the brand arrived in Britain in 2021, with other sites in London, Manchester, Birmingham, Reading, Essex, Basingstoke, Northampton and Glasgow. The company was founded in Australia in 2005 and now has more than 350 locations worldwide.

For town-centre businesses, a new food outlet within reach of the colleges adds to the lunchtime trade around Mellor Street. Have you tried it yet, and what other food or shops would you like to see open in the town centre? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: Rochdale Asda worker's kindness a 'breath of fresh air' for widowed customer
articles.excerpt: Shaheda times her help around an older customer's shopping trips after the woman lost her husband, scanning and packing her shopping and stopping for a chat.
articles.content_html:
A worker at Asda's Rochdale store has been praised for looking out for an older customer after the woman was widowed.

Shaheda first noticed something had changed when the customer, who used to shop with her husband, stopped coming in for a while. When she next saw her, the woman was shopping with her daughter, and the pair told her what had happened.

The daughter lives in London and was worried about how her mother would cope on her own. Shaheda promised to look after her and told her which days she works, so the customer could time her visits for when Shaheda would be there.

Now, when the customer comes in, Shaheda scans and packs her shopping, fetches her a chair and makes time for a chat.

The customer told the store's customer manager, Dave, how much the help meant to her. Dave said: "The lady told me that ever since she lost her husband three months ago, Shaheda has been like a breath of fresh air in her life every time she shops – not just because of the help she offers, but as an emotional support and somebody to chat to."

Shaheda said: "I used to see the lady come in with her husband all the time and then didn't see her for a while. Then I saw her shopping with her daughter, and they told me what had happened. I told her to come and see me every time she came in... and she does. We have a good chat and I help her, as she does struggle a bit."

She added: "She thanks me every single time and I go, 'no, you don't need to thank me'. It's sweet, though. I like to think that somebody would do that for my own mum. I always think too that one day I could be in that position. It doesn't cost anything to be pleasant and kind, does it?"

For someone adjusting to life alone after a bereavement, a familiar face on a weekly errand can make a real difference, and the help Shaheda gives costs nothing but a little time.

articles.title: Investigation works begin at former Turner Brothers factory site in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Spodden Park Ltd has started investigations to locate buried asbestos at the derelict Turner Brothers factory, aiming for future redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
Spodden Park Ltd has commenced investigation works at the former Turner Brothers factory site in Spotland, Rochdale, to locate buried asbestos.

This site, once the world’s largest producer of asbestos, has been a concern for local residents due to the toxic materials associated with its history.

The investigations will be carried out by a specialist contractor over the coming weeks. Spodden Park Ltd assures that no asbestos will be disturbed during this phase, which aims to inform a safe remediation strategy for the site.

Heavy machinery will be used, but the company has stated that no buildings will be demolished during this process.

articles.title: Rochdale driver jailed for 16 months after dangerous police pursuit
articles.excerpt: Bilal Ishaq admitted four driving offences after a pursuit through Rochdale. Police say he ran red lights and twice tried to reverse into pursuing vehicles.
articles.content_html:
A disqualified driver who fled police through Rochdale has been jailed for 16 months and banned from driving for five years.

Bilal Ishaq, 34, of Hey Street, Rochdale, pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, failing to stop and driving without insurance, Greater Manchester Police said in a release issued on 2 November.

Officers had tried to stop a vehicle on Foxholes Road in September. GMP said the vehicle was linked to suspected drug dealing. The offences set out in the force’s sentencing announcement were driving offences.

Ishaq drove away, beginning a pursuit through the town. According to police, he reached speeds more than three times the limit, went through red lights and drove on the wrong side of the road.

The force said he also tried to reverse into pursuing police vehicles on two occasions. After crashing, he attempted to run away but was detained by officers.

GMP said Ishaq was already subject to two driving disqualifications imposed in January 2026 following a separate dangerous driving incident in December 2025.

PC Matt Balkwell, from the force’s Motorcycle Unit, said: “His actions could easily have resulted in serious injury or loss of life.”

The officer praised the work of those involved in detaining Ishaq and said police would continue to pursue drivers who endangered their communities.

articles.title: Sandbrook Way KFC licence now permits late-night service until 5am
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's public licensing register shows updated permission for late-night refreshment at the Sandbrook Way KFC, with the restaurant area due to close at midnight under a licence condition.
articles.content_html:
The KFC at Sandbrook Way, Edinburgh Way, Rochdale, has a premises licence permitting late-night refreshment until 5am on every day of the week, according to Rochdale Borough Council's public licensing register.

The register identifies the premises as KFC, OL11 1RY, and names Chicken Cabins Ltd trading as KFC as the licence holder. It lists licence PL(N)1021 with an effective date of 17 October 2026. The permitted premises hours are shown as 10am to 5am, while late-night refreshment is authorised from 11pm to 5am, indoors and outdoors.

There is an important distinction between the permission and what customers can expect on any particular night. The licence sets out what is legally authorised; it is not a verified announcement that every service is operating throughout those hours. A condition in the published record says the restaurant area is to close at midnight, with delivery and drive-through service afterwards.

An earlier version of the same council record, viewed as at 11 October 2026, listed midnight closing on most days and 1am on Friday and Saturday. The updated register therefore records a materially later authorised finish time. It does not explain the commercial reasons for the change or give a launch date for extended service.

The licence includes conditions covering CCTV, door supervision during late-night licensing hours, management of noise and litter, and requests for customers to leave quietly. These are licence requirements, not evidence of a specific incident at the premises.

Customers wanting to know whether collection, drive-through or delivery is currently available after midnight should check directly with the restaurant. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the operator confirms its actual trading timetable.

articles.title: New plans for Greggs bakery at Littleborough Service Station
articles.excerpt: Motor Fuel Group has submitted a planning application to Rochdale Council to establish a Greggs bakery at Littleborough Service Station, creating new jobs and utilising existing buildings.
articles.content_html:
Motor Fuel Group has submitted a planning application to Rochdale Council to establish a Greggs bakery at Littleborough Service Station on Church Street.

The proposal involves reconfiguring the existing jet-wash building to create a new shop with a single-storey front extension, while changing the use of the current shop to a retail bakery.

This new application follows a previous one submitted in October last year, which proposed demolishing the car-wash building to make way for a new bakery pod. However, that plan was withdrawn on June 30, as it was deemed unnecessary to demolish the existing structure.

The current proposal aims to make more efficient use of the existing buildings on site, retaining the established petrol filling station use.

If approved, the development is expected to create four full-time and four part-time jobs, contributing to local employment. JMS Planning, representing Motor Fuel Group, stated that the revised proposal is similar to the previous one but focuses on utilising existing facilities rather than demolition.

The application is currently under consideration by Rochdale Council, and local residents will be keen to see how this development could enhance the service station's offerings and potentially improve convenience for customers.

articles.title: Asda worker Saheda Bibi praised for supporting widowed customer in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Saheda Bibi, an Asda employee in Rochdale, has been recognised for her kindness in helping a recently widowed customer with her shopping needs.
articles.content_html:
An Asda employee in Rochdale has received praise for her compassionate support of a recently widowed customer. Saheda Bibi, 43, has worked at the store since 2012 and made a promise to look after the woman after learning about her loss.

The customer’s daughter, who lives in London, expressed concern about how her mother would manage alone following her husband's death. Saheda reassured her by sharing her work schedule, allowing the daughter to plan her mother's shopping trips accordingly.

Since then, Saheda has assisted the woman with her shopping, ensuring she has a chair to sit on and taking the time to chat with her.

The customer was so grateful for Saheda's kindness that she contacted the store's customer manager, Dave Jeffs, to express her appreciation.

In recognition of her outstanding service, Dave has nominated Saheda for an Asda Service Superstar Award, highlighting the positive impact she has made on the customer's life during a difficult time.

articles.title: Rochdale reception school applications for 2027: deadline, preferences and offer dates
articles.excerpt: Parents applying for a Rochdale borough reception place starting September 2027 have until 15 January. The council has also confirmed the offer date and rules for school preferences.
articles.content_html:
Applications for reception places at Rochdale borough primary schools for September 2027 are open, with parents and carers given until Friday, 15 January 2027 to apply on time.

Rochdale Borough Council opened its online admissions system on 14 September 2026. The council says parents should submit their application before the January closing date; otherwise, it will be treated as late. National offer day for reception places is Friday, 16 April 2027, when families can find out which school has been offered.

Parents are encouraged to name five different schools in their order of preference. Listing only one school does not improve the chance of being offered that school. If it is oversubscribed, the published admissions criteria are applied; where a preferred school cannot be offered, the council considers the other preferences and available places.

The council advises families to check each school's admissions policy before applying. The rules for community and voluntary controlled schools are not necessarily the same as those for academies, foundation or voluntary aided schools. Attending a school's nursery class does not normally guarantee priority for its reception class. Some schools also ask parents to submit supplementary forms directly to the school.

For families who move house after applying, the council lists Friday, 12 February 2027 as the final date for address changes to be considered in the initial allocation, subject to the required evidence. Changes of school preference after the application deadline are treated as late.

Parents considering deferring their child's start should still apply by 15 January. The council explains that the rules depend on the child's birthday, and applications for a place outside the normal age group require supporting evidence and an individual decision by the admission authority.

Children living in Rochdale borough apply through Rochdale Borough Council even when choosing a school outside the borough. Families who live elsewhere must apply through their own council. The school admissions team can be contacted at school.admissions@rochdale.gov.uk or 0300 303 0340.

Full dates, admissions guidance and the application route are published at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/school-admissions-appeals/apply-primary-school-place. Families can also consult the council's guidance before choosing schools at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/school-admissions-appeals/apply-primary-school-place/3.

articles.title: Rochdale's Atom Valley project aims to create thousands of jobs and homes
articles.excerpt: The Atom Valley development aims to create 17 million square feet of employment space and 7,000 new homes in Rochdale, with the first phase already underway.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is set to undergo a significant transformation with the announcement of the Atom Valley development, which aims to create 17 million square feet of employment space and 7,000 new homes.

This ambitious project is expected to generate around 20,000 highly skilled jobs in the technology and manufacturing sectors, addressing the town's long-standing issues of low wages and lost investment.

The development is spearheaded by the Rochdale Development Agency, led by managing director Rachel Laver, who emphasised the importance of making local residents aware of the opportunities that Atom Valley will bring.

Laver stated, "I want to do more of bringing what we do closer to people," highlighting the need for community engagement in the project.

The first milestone of the Atom Valley initiative was the completion of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park, which is now equipped to attract international businesses.

This centre is seen as a crucial step towards revitalising the local economy and changing perceptions about job opportunities in Rochdale.

As the project progresses, local residents and businesses are encouraged to engage with the developments.

The RDA aims to ensure that the benefits of Atom Valley are felt by the community, fostering growth and reducing the need for residents to seek employment opportunities outside of Rochdale.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The multi-billion plan to transform Rochdale - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The multi-billion plan to transform Rochdale Boasting stunning Pennine views and 20-minute train links to Manchester, Rochdale has long struggled with low wages and lost investment. Sitting down with the M.E.N., development boss Rachel Laver outlines how Atom Valley and station linear parks will finally make the town's wealth stay put. View 8 Images Rochdale town centre. (Image: Rochdale Council) Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter 16:59, 01 Nov 2026 Updated 12:12, 02 Nov 2026 Rochdale has trams, trains, motorway links as well as stunning views of the Pennines and a rich cultural and historic heritage. It has everything you’d expect of an area with the ability to thrive, so why it has lower than average salaries and high deprivation is a puzzling question. But things are changing in the north-eastern borough of Greater Manchester. The civic centre, Rochdale town centre, has already undergone a major facelift. Yet there is more to come for the town, with plans to link up the town to its train station. To get the very latest from Manchester's political scene in your newsfeed - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source ‌ The Atom Valley development zone is on the way, which is estimated to bring 17m sq ft employment space, 7,000 new homes and offer 20,000 ‘highly skilled’ roles in the technology and manufacturing sectors. The first tangible milestone of Atom Valley arrived earlier this month when the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) was completed in the Northern Gateway part of the project. It now stands proud at Kingsway Business Park, ready to be kitted out with all the technology needed to house international innovative businesses and manufacturers. View 8 Images Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale where ground was broken on new Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News) Atom Valley was even described by Prime Minister Andy Burnham as the start of a ‘new decade of growth’ in Greater Manchester during his days as the city-region’s mayor. ‌ But many won’t have heard of the organisation behind a majority of these major projects - Rochdale Development Agency. It is a reasonable assumption to say the RDA are the construction arm of Rochdale council because if there is a council-led building project, it’s likely to be the RDA delivering it. However, the RDA’s recently appointed managing director, Rachel Laver, said there are many more strings to their bow - or perhaps more accurately, more excavators to their diggers. Rachel sat down with the Manchester Evening News and divulged her lofty ambitions for Rochdale. View 8 Images Rachel Laver, managing director of the Rochdale Development Agency (Image: RDA) ‌ The popular misquote of ‘build it and they will come’ from the 1989 film Field of Dreams has become part of common vernacular. In a nutshell, that is exactly how the RDA boss feels about the future of Rochdale. Rachel said: “I want to do more of bringing what we do closer to people. We talk about Northern Gateway and Atom Valley, a huge initiative bigger than Trafford Park and a collaboration between Bury , Oldham and Rochdale councils. “But I want local people to know it’s for them, not just some nebulous thing you hear people talking about. “I think we need to bring Northern Gateway and Atom Valley closer to the people of Rochdale so they can see there are job opportunities there. ‌ “We want businesses to come to Rochdale but we want businesses in Rochdale to grow.” Don't let an algorithm decide what Manchester news you see - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source The RDA boss felt her job was to work with businesses and organisations to create opportunity. She explained there is this feeling that if you want to be successful, you have to leave Rochdale. Atom Valley is one of the big projects that she hopes can change that mindset by providing high skilled jobs locally - and lots of them. But she highlighted there are some manufacturers in the area already doing that, such as Heatsense Cables making parts for space rockets and Hutchinson Engineering who make parts for JCB and Caterpillar. ‌ “You listen to the press and you’d think manufacturing is dead, it’s not,” said Rachel. “Manufacturers are doing amazingly well. “Rochdale has a manufacturing history and we still have those ties.” She wants to see greater space and funding to provide growth for businesses. Rachel explained that funding pots often go for the ‘low hanging fruit’ and give it to the big cities. That is a big downfall for Rochdale in her eyes - that it’s not a city centre like Manchester. “Quite often the funding goes into the main centres and the areas on the periphery don’t get as much investment,” Rachel added. “So I think we need to bang the drum to make sure we get our fair share.” ‌ View 8 Images Baillie Street in Rochdale town centre (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News) According to her data, ‘£10 goes around the economy two times in Rochdale’, compared to a well-functioning economy where it goes around seven times. This means that if a project is started, the contract for that job may go to a company outside the area and employ other people from outside the area - and the money goes with them to benefit another local economy. So making the £10 go around the economy more times would mean more local businesses winning contracts, employing local people and providing more apprenticeships and training for young people. With more and more young people not in education, employment, or training (NEETs), Rachel explained pushing for more apprenticeships and training is vital for upskilling the next generation in Rochdale. ‌ Focusing on getting the ‘£10 around more times’ is something she believes will help boost the local economy in the long run. But in order to attract outside investment into Atom Valley, Rochdale needs a ‘whole package’, Rachel adds. This is why there is a plan for thousands of new homes to be built around Atom Valley and why the RDA is lobbying with Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) to increase tram regularity, new bus timetables and improve the road network. View 8 Images The new Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale (Image: RDA) There is already work happening on the Simister Island upgrade, coming in 2029 and in 2023, getting the Queen Elizabeth II Way extension off Junction 19 in South Heywood has proved vital for access to businesses in that area. ‌ Rachel said that affordable housing is important and understands why, politically, it is a big thing to deliver. But she says ‘aspirational housing’ is also needed to attract the high-earning clientele that would come with the Atom Valley project. She believes there is so much the borough could offer for executive homes - views of the Pennines, wonderful greenery and brilliant transport connections to Yorkshire and Manchester city centre . It takes less than 20 minutes to get to Manchester Victoria by train. The RDA boss went onto how they are helping to deliver this ‘full package’ - through making the town centre more vibrant and, simply, a nicer place to be. They are already taking action on this by starting on a housing project right next to Rochdale station. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place , in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. ‌ It will be followed by a revamp of the station, including a new project called ‘Station Platform Gardens’, which will bring life and greenery back to the disused platform. Currently there are just ‘steps that go to nowhere’ at the station, Rachel explained. View 8 Images The former Central Retail Park site development under construction (Image: Rochdale council) She continued: “At the moment I think the station feels really disconnected from the town centre. As you go down Drake Street it isn’t very welcoming. “As we build up John Rennie Place, it’s going to get so much more footfall, which uplifts the area. Then people invest when you’ve got the footfall as well. ‌ “Excitingly and innovatively, we’re leading on a project called Station Platform Gardens. There is a redundant station platform at Rochdale, so we’re going to create a linear park. “That will have healthy walks. But on the other side of the station, the park and ride will be turned into a multi-storey car park and that whole area will be redeveloped.” The area in front of the station will eventually be shut off to traffic and have a plaza there - ‘a whole different feel’. Rachel adds that ‘it will be a much better welcome to Rochdale’ a true gateway you’d expect when arriving by train. Another role the RDA plays is in culture and heritage - running around 54 programmes across the borough. ‌ RDA also operates Grade-I listed Rochdale Town Hall and the Touchstones museum and art gallery across the Esplanade. Touchstones will be reopened in Spring 2027, Rachel revealed. View 8 Images Rochdale Town Hall (Image: Rochdale Council) But it isn’t just Rochdale getting all the love, the outside towns are all seeing big projects coming forward. In Middleton, there is the Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) moving forwards . This will see the council buying out Warwick Mill so it can finally be redeveloped. Rachel said there had been some costly realisations when it came to the abandoned spinning mill - with around 1,500 tyres found dumped there. ‌ The cost of properly disposing of tyres is most likely the reason for this fly-tipping, but it’s now a cost the local authority will have to bear once it finalises the deal to take over the site later this year. Outside of that, the RDA will also be helping support the delivery of the MDC, which aims to bring Metrolink trams to Middleton ; create new homes on brownfield plots; build high-quality business premises; and better public areas, roads and pathways. View 8 Images Warwick Mill in Middleton (Image: Rochdale council) When asked how Rochdale will look in 10 years time, Rachel said: “I would like to say we’d see thriving communities. But we should see more town centres living across the whole of the borough, not just Rochdale. ‌ “The borough as a whole has the capacity to take a lot of housing. We know the government has set very high housing targets and Manchester city centre is struggling for space. “We can take the housing. So 7,000 new homes are proposed in Atom Valley and I think all that investment will support the local economy. We will get £10 going around the economy far more. “I’m really excited about the SMMC and Atom Valley and the types of businesses we could have here. It is creating that cluster which will give us strength and opportunities that people don’t need to move away from Rochdale. “We want young people in Rochdale to aspire to be the best, but we want them to come back. ‌ “We want people to be proud of Rochdale and shouting and saying ‘come, because it’s great’. Because it genuinely is. “I think it will look different in 10 years time. articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards contract for family temporary accommodation services
articles.excerpt: The Bond Board Limited has been awarded a contract to manage the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme, providing vital support to homeless families in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract for the management and support services of the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme (HFLS) to The Bond Board Limited. This initiative aims to provide essential tenancy management and support for homeless families placed in temporary accommodation.

The HFLS will oversee approximately 40 leased properties, offering services that include property management, tenancy sustainment, and move-on support. This contract is part of the council's ongoing efforts to address homelessness in the area and provide stable housing solutions for families in need.

In addition to the HFLS contract, the council has also awarded a separate contract for the A Bed for Every Night (ABEN) Dispersed Accommodation and Support Services to Stepping Stone Projects.

This service will provide around 34 units of accommodation for homeless individuals and those at risk of rough sleeping, along with housing-related support to help them achieve stable living conditions.

These contracts are significant steps in tackling homelessness in Rochdale, reflecting the council's commitment to supporting vulnerable families and individuals. The Bond Board Limited and Stepping Stone Projects are expected to begin their services shortly, contributing to the local community's efforts to reduce homelessness.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale has celebrated a successful year at the North West in Bloom awards, achieving 21 gold awards and multiple category wins, including Best Town Centre.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has celebrated a remarkable achievement at the North West in Bloom awards, securing 21 gold awards and eight overall category wins.

The results were announced during the annual ceremony held at Toughsheet Community Stadium in Bolton on 30 October 2026, following visits from Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) judges over the summer.

The awards highlight the borough's commitment to horticulture, environmental responsibility, and community participation. Rochdale town centre's horticulturists continued their winning streak, taking gold and the title of Best Town Centre, alongside their success at the recent RHS Britain in Bloom awards.

Phil Massey, treasurer of Rochdale in Bloom, received an outstanding contribution award for his significant efforts in supporting the borough's success.

The Baillie Street Quarter won the new Best Art in the Community award for its artwork from the Common Walls International Mural Festival, led by local artist Hayley Garner.

Other notable winners included the Hampton by Hilton hotel, which won gold in its category, and Heywood town centre, which also achieved gold thanks to the efforts of local volunteers.

The success of Rochdale in Bloom not only showcases the borough's beauty but also fosters community pride and environmental awareness.

articles.title: Rochdale Council approves new Storage World building in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for a new Storage World building in Middleton, following a fire that destroyed the previous structure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has approved the rebuilding of Storage World in Middleton town centre. The planning application submitted by Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd (SSPMI) was greenlit to replace the building on Old Hall Street, which was destroyed by fire in June last year.

The new development will be a £12 million mixed-use building, smaller in footprint but taller than the previous structure.

It will feature self-storage units on the upper floors and commercial units on the ground floor, occupying half the space of the former Storage World but with two additional storeys to maintain capacity.

In their application, P4 Planning highlighted the aim to create a modern design that would not only restore self-storage services but also stimulate small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) activity in the area.

They noted that the design would reflect the historical context of the site, which previously housed Albany Mill until 1975.

This development is expected to contribute positively to the regeneration of Middleton town centre, enhancing the local economy and providing much-needed facilities for residents and businesses alike.

Winstanley, who co-runs the Manchester-based theatre company The Performers’ Playground with Alice Robinson, has a rich history in theatre, having performed nationally and internationally with various touring companies.

In addition to 'Cabaret Schmabaret', The Performers’ Playground is also fundraising for a separate production of 'Ubu Royale', which is currently in research and development. This production is designed to accommodate Winstanley's mobility and fatigue issues, with plans for a national tour in 2027.

Winstanley's comeback not only highlights his personal journey but also serves as an inspiration for others facing similar challenges. Local audiences can look forward to enjoying a unique comedic experience while supporting a talented artist's return to the stage.

articles.title: Did goblins move Rochdale Parish Church up the hill?
articles.excerpt: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.summary: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.body:
The short answer is: no, there is no evidence that goblins or other supernatural creatures physically moved the stones of St Chad’s Church. That story belongs to Lancashire folklore, best known from the 19th‑century collector John Roby, while the documentary and architectural record shows a long‑standing church site with medieval fabric and later restorations. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

Roby’s version of the tale — titled “The Goblin Builders” in his Traditions of Lancashire — describes a Saxon thane, piles of building stone laid by the river, and those materials mysteriously transferred overnight to the hill where St Chad’s now stands; Roby also notes the famous flight of steps (he records 124) leading up to the church. That account is a clear piece of local storytelling rather than a contemporary record of building work. Roby wrote in the 19th century as a folklorist and compiler of oral tradition; his retelling preserves how people in his era understood the place, not the legal or archaeological history of its masoning. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

The documented history of the building is plain and far less sensational. Historic England lists St Chad’s as Grade II* and describes medieval and post‑medieval construction phases: a thirteenth‑century tower, fourteenth‑century arcade columns and arches, a clerestory dated 1557, and substantial Victorian restorations and additions in the 19th century. Those layers — Norman and medieval masonry altered, repaired and refashioned over centuries — explain the church’s position and appearance more plausibly than an overnight relocation by invisible hands. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

Why on the hill? Practical and symbolic reasons usually guided medieval siting. A high position overlooks the river and the town, keeps the building clear of floodplain, and gives the church civic and visual prominence; these are the kinds of factors architectural historians use when they discuss hilltop parish churches, and they match the description of St Chad’s occupying high ground above the River Roch. The building’s long use as the mother church of the ancient parish of Rochdale — serving a large rural parish for many centuries — also favoured a prominent site. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

That is not to say the legend has no local value. Roby’s telling and other versions preserve a communal memory that the church’s siting felt important enough to explain with a story; the goblin motif is widespread in English folklore as a way to name unexplained or surprising events. Local guides and walking routes still point out the steps and repeat the tale; it’s part of how Rochdale people have talked about their church across generations. But folklore and documentary history are different tools: the former explains meaning, the latter records evidence. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

If you want to check the facts in person: the parish continues to use St Chad’s as Rochdale Parish Church, and the building, its steps and the churchyard are publicly accessible; the parish’s information pages list services and contact details. For the architectural inventory, Historic England’s official list entry gives the formal description and dating used by planners and conservators. If any reader is curious about the Roby story itself, his Traditions of Lancashire is available in full online as a 19th‑century account of local legend. ([rochdalecommunity.org.uk](https://rochdalecommunity.org.uk/sites/saint-chad-rochdale-parish-church/))

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.summary: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.body:
Short answer: the house at Clegg Hall is real; the boggart belongs to folklore.

Clegg Hall stands on Clegg Hall Road, near Smithy Bridge (Milnrow) about two miles north‑east of Rochdale. The building you can see today is a protected, Grade II* listed house whose main fabric dates to about 1610; Historic England records that listing (List Entry 1309615, first listed 10 August 1951) and gives the architectural description and location. Those are verifiable, recent and public facts. The “boggart” stories are an older, oral and literary tradition layered over that solid record. 

What the documents say: local and county histories trace the place-name and family back to the medieval era but do not confirm the grisly crime the legend describes.
